report:
## Conclusion

**Yes, denosumab (Prolia) significantly reduces the risk of vertebral fractures in osteoporosis.** The evidence is strong and consistent across multiple high-quality sources.

### Key Evidence

The pivotal **FREEDOM trial** (published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, 2009) is the landmark Phase 3 study that led to FDA approval of denosumab. In this randomized, placebo-controlled trial of nearly 7,900 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, denosumab (60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months for 36 months) reduced the risk of new radiographic vertebral fractures by **68%** relative to placebo (cumulative incidence 2.3% vs. 7.2%). It also reduced hip fractures by 40% and nonvertebral fractures by 20% ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0809493)).

A **10-year extension study** published in *The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology* confirmed sustained fracture risk reduction, with yearly incidence of vertebral fractures remaining low (0.90–1.86%) over the extension period, similar to rates during the original trial ([Lancet](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(17)30138-9/fulltext)).

A **network meta-analysis** published in *BMJ* (2023) found that denosumab was among the most effective treatments for reducing vertebral fractures compared with placebo, and a separate network meta-analysis suggested denosumab may be more effective than bisphosphonates for vertebral fracture prevention (RR 0.62; 95% CI) ([BMJ](https://www.bmj.com/content/381/bmj-2021-068033); [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6447951/)).

### Important Caveat
If denosumab is discontinued, patients should promptly transition to an alternative antiresorptive therapy, as stopping treatment is associated with a rebound increase in vertebral fracture risk, including multiple vertebral fractures.

**Bottom line:** Denosumab is a well-established, evidence-based treatment that substantially reduces vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women and men with osteoporosis.
